mappings.note: Rainfall case study: a thin layer over a roof is collected as a cylinder of water, and the depth follows from equating the two. Conversion of a volume from one shape to another.

Harvesting case study: rain over the roof's PLAN area is stored in a cylindrical tank. Same volume-conservation reasoning, so the conversion outcome and not a combination. (Roof dimensions are only in a figure the stem does not carry.)
Advertising column = cylinder with a hemispherical cap; the poster and paint areas are the curved surfaces added, the shared circle being hidden. Surface area of a combination.
Milk tanker case study: the tanker's contents are split and poured into a cuboidal and a cylindrical vessel, each level following from the transferred volume's new shape.
A spherical scoop MELTS into a cone: will it overflow, and what percentage fills. The comparison only makes sense because volume is conserved through the change of shape.
Surface area of the Earth as a single sphere, computed from two different diameters and their mean. One basic solid, no combination and no conversion.

Volume and surface area of one sphere, then fixed percentages of each. Single-solid mensuration; the percentages come from a survey graphic the stem does not carry, so the item is not answerable as printed.
Pantheon = cylinder plus hemispherical dome; interior volume is the two added, with the wall height deduced from the total height. Volume of a combination.

Ball bearings counted by dividing a box's stated capacity by one sphere's volume, with a mm-to-cm step and a mass chain. Nothing is melted, so C-7.3-LO-3 is wrong; the content is single-solid volume and units.

Cone on a cylinder of SMALLER diameter, so the cylinder's top ring stays exposed; the painting areas must be assembled face by face. Surface area of a combination, and the unequal radii are what make it non-routine.
A cuboidal tank and a cylindrical tank sized and compared as two separate solids. They are never joined into one body, so neither combination outcome applies.

Excavation volume is a plain cylinder (C-7.2), but the last part coats only the MAJOR ARC above a chord with angle AOB = 90 degrees, which is a 270-degree sector/arc computation - the one place in this chapter where C-7.1 is genuinely earned.

A spherical lump of mixture becomes a cylindrical biscuit; the volume DIFFERENCE is the trapped air. It is the conversion outcome with the conservation deliberately broken, which no combination outcome describes.
Conical-bottom tank asks both capacity (cylinder + cone volumes, LO-3) and the sheet needed (flat top + curved cylinder + curved cone, LO-2). Two parts, two outcomes.

Part (i) literally asks which EXPRESSION is correct for the surface of a cylinder with two hemispherical ends, i.e. selecting each component's formula and noticing the flat ends are not exposed (C-7.1-LO-4); the total 10 pi r^2 is then the composite surface (C-7.2-LO-2).
Kumbh tent: the cylindrical wall and the conical top are costed at DIFFERENT rates, so each component's curved surface must be found separately before totalling. Surface area of a combination.
